title: Traveling, and saying goodbye
goal: Handle hotels and travel, deal with small problems on the road, and close the course with goodbye phrases.

dialogs.title: Elkarrizketa — Hotelean, Donostian
dialogs.intro: Budi's last trip before going home to Indonesia. He arrives at the front desk of a small hotel near the beach.

lines.speaker: Harreragilea:
lines.id: Good afternoon! Do you have a reservation?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Bai, Budi Santoso izenean. Bi gauetarako.
lines.id: Yes, under the name Budi Santoso. For two nights.
lines.literal: yes, Budi Santoso name-in. two night-pl-for.

lines.speaker: Harreragilea:
lines.text: Bai, hemen dago. Hogeita bat gela, bigarren solairuan.
lines.id: Yes, here it is. Room twenty-one, second floor.
lines.literal: yes, here is. twenty-and one room, second floor-on.

lines.speaker: Harreragilea:
lines.id: Yes, from eight to ten, on the ground floor.

lines.speaker: Harreragilea:
lines.id: Yes, the password is on the card.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Eskerrik asko. Bihar goiz irten behar dut.
lines.id: Thank you. I have to leave early tomorrow.
lines.literal: thanks many. tomorrow early leave need I-have-it.

lines.speaker: Harreragilea:
lines.text: Ez dago arazorik. Giltza hemen duzu.
lines.literal: not is problem-any. key-the here you-have.

lines.speaker: Harreragilea:
lines.text: Ez, bost minutu oinez. Kaletik zuzen.
lines.id: No, five minutes on foot. Straight down this street.
lines.literal: no, five minute foot-by. street-from straight.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Primeran. Eskerrik asko, oso jatorra zara!
lines.id: Great. Thank you, you're very kind!
lines.literal: great. thanks many, very kind-the you-are!

notes: **Bi gauetarako — for two nights.** A combination of three endings you already know: *gau* + *-eta-* (plural) + *-rako* (for). Other forms with the same pattern: *hiru egunetarako* (for three days), *aste baterako* (for a week).

**Izenean — under the name.** *Budi izenean* (under the name Budi). *Izen* means name, and *-ean* is the place ending you've used since Unit 3. Basque says "in the name" where English says "under the name".

**Wifirik badago? — the ending -rik again.** In questions about something that may or may not exist, the thing takes *-rik*: *wifirik*, *gelarik*, *lekurik*. It's the same ending you learned in Units 4 and 5 — and by now it should feel natural.
**Ez dago arazorik — no problem.** One of those short phrases that keep a conversation flowing. Similar ones: *lasai* (relax, don't worry), *berdin dio* (doesn't matter), *noski* (of course).

blocks.text: *Euritakoa* literally means "the one for rain" — an umbrella. The *-tako* pattern is productive: *eguzkitakoa* (the one for the sun), *bidaiatakoa*. Once you recognize the word pieces, many long Basque words stop feeling foreign.

blocks.title: Numbers and places to note down
items: **112** — the emergency number for everything: ambulance, police, fire department.
*Udaltzaingoa* — city police; *Ertzaintza* — the Basque regional police.
*Galdutako gauzen bulegoa* — lost and found office.
*Turismo bulegoa* — tourist information office; there's almost always staff who speak Basque, Spanish, French, and English.
*Anbulatorioa* — general clinic; *larrialdiak* — emergency room.

blocks.text: You've reached the end of twenty units. Let's count what you can now do in a language whose sounds you may never have heard six months ago.

items: Introduce yourself and say where you're from, your age, your job, and your family.
Order food and drinks, go shopping, and ask about prices.
Tell the time, name days and months, and plan a schedule.
Describe daily activities, habits, and what you're doing right now.
Ask for directions, say where things are, and travel by train or bus.
Say what you like and don't like, and invite other people.
Talk about yesterday and the weekend that's just gone.
Make plans for tomorrow, next week, and next year.
And most important: use the doer's hat *-k* and the three auxiliary patterns without stopping to think too long.

blocks.title: Three things you can start doing tomorrow
items: **Listen every day.** The radio station *Euskadi Irratia* and the TV channel *EITB* broadcast in Basque all day; children's shows are the easiest to follow. Twenty minutes a day is enough.
**Reread this course from Unit 1.** The second reading feels different: what once looked like rules now reads like sentences. It isn't repetition — it's the next step.

**Use it, even with mistakes.** No euskara speaker will correct you harshly — the language has too few speakers to turn away anyone who tries. One *kaixo* and one *eskerrik asko* already open the door.
